catalog_locator: p. 23 (Phonology: definition and inventory of tone); language key p. 6 ('language N: Nde language O: Nselle language P: Nta'); informants p. 7 (Nde: Agbor Akanya Agbor of Mbenkpin; Nselle: Matthew Abobo Agbor of Njemetop); Nde tonal minimal pair p. 28 (nam 'disappear' vs nâm 'cook'). Whole-volume search: 'stress' 0 hits (Google Books search-within id 3-4fSw3dkTQC, saved) and Crabb not returned for '"Njemetop" stress' in the archive.org open full-text index (re-run) - two independent scan layers.
catalog_quote: TONE is here defined as the distribution of vocal tension over the syllable. Since its domain is fixed, i.e. the syllable, and since this domain is necessarily greater than a single segment in at least some cases, then tone is considered as an element of the structure rather than of any segment. On the other hand, tone also has a LOCUS within the syllable determined on contrastive grounds. When two utterances such as fèb and fêb ('fan it' and 'jump') are contrasted, it is precisely the syllabic centre, the most prominent part of the syllable which alone is capable of bearing the contrast. Therefore, this part of the syllable, which is the syllable peak in Hockett's terms, is regarded as the TONE-BEARING segment ... Every nucleus must bear a tone, of which there are four contrastive possibilities in the Ekoid Bantu Languages. These possibilities are: 1. High: a level of relatively greatest vocal tension; 2. Low: a level (or a rapidly fading level, if final) of relatively lessened vocal tension; 3. Falling: a rapid lessening of vocal tension from an initial level of some high intensity; and 4. Rising: a rapid increase of vocal tension, or a maintaining the original level if final. To these four possibilities a fifth has been added, especially in languages N, O, P, T, and U on grounds of dia-phonemic contrast: 5. Mid: a level of relatively greater vocal tension. These tones are symbolized as follows: 1. High: an acute accent placed over the tone-bearing segment ...
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress
sweep_summary: nden1250 Nde-Nsele-Nta (Ekoid, Nigeria) is not in the catalog. Every one of the 71 works with stress in the title is a Glottolog 5.1 record whose language code is 'Nde-Nsele-Nta [ndd] (computerized assignment from "words")' - checked for all 71 ids in the local sources.bib copy - and all concern other languages (English, Dutch, Portuguese, Turkish/French, Nahuatl, Chinese, Japanese, Indonesian, Russian, German, Faroese, Kaqchikel, Lushootseed, Saisiyat, sign languages) or general theory/acquisition; none was downloaded (priority none). Beyond the list: archive.org full-text searches for Ekoid/Nde/Nselle/Nta/Bakor/Ekajuk + stress (11 hit files saved) surface no stress statement for Nde-Nsele-Nta; Ethnologue scans give only population, dialects and classification for [ndd]; Crabb 1965, the sole phonology covering Nde (N), Nselle (O), Nta (P), describes tone only (H, L, F, R + Mid) and contains no token 'stress' in two independent scanned indexes (snippet access only; medium priority to read in full). The only Ekoid stress statement located and read is Watters 2001 (Research Mate in African Linguistics, p. 67) for the sister language Ejagham: root-initial, no pitch/loudness correlate, not phonologically significant - saved from the open archive.org djvu text under and logged in, useful for ejag1239, not for this language. no new stress statement was found.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Nde (N), Nselle (O) and Nta (P) are described as lexical-tone lects with five contrastive syllable tones (High, Mid, Low, Falling, Rising; the Mid tone posited specifically for N, O, P, Nnam and Ekajuk); the only phonological description covering these lects never mentions stress or accent (0 hits for 'stress' in the volume), and no source states a word-stress position.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Crabb notes falling tones on 'coordinate nuclei' are split across two segments (p.25) and that plural tone changes in sub-group m-p (Efutop, Nde, Nselle, Nta) were deferred to the never-published Part 2 (p.71).
new_statements.domain_note: Tone domain = the syllable (tone-bearing segment = syllable peak); data are citation-form comparative vocabulary items elicited from one speaker per lect (Nde: Mbenkpin; Nselle: Njemetop). Access caveat: passage reconstructed from overlapping Google Books snippets (scanned), not from a full page scan.
new_statements.identity_note: Crabb 1965 treats the three lects separately as 'language N: Nde' (Glottolog dialect ndee1242), 'language O: Nselle' (nsel1238) and 'language P: Nta' (ntaa1242) (p.6); his tone remark on p.23 names exactly N, O, P (plus T = Nnam, U = Ekajuk). Nselle informant from Njemetop, Nde informant from Mbenkpin (p.7). The Glottolog 'glottolog_refs' list supplied for this key (Tallman 2020, Storkel 2013, etc.) is spurious: all 1,666 such entries in sources.bib carry language code 'Nde-Nsele-Nta [ndd] (computerized assignment from "words")'; the genuine Glottolog holdings for [ndd] are wordlists/overviews only (Glottolog's fullest description is only a wordlist).
